newsitem.title: CONGO: Troops clash with ex-leader's men in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Troops clash with ex-leader's men in Brazzaville.

text.p: Government troops clashed with supporters of former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso on Thursday in Brazzaville, capital of the oil-producing former French colony of Congo.

Witnesses said shooting spread through Sassou Nguesso's stronghold in the northern suburbs and that the army, loyal to President Pascal Lissouba, had sent reinforcements. They said four people were wounded, two by stray bullets.
Sassou Nguesso, interviewed by Radio France International, accused Lissouba of surrounding his home with tanks and seeking an excuse to postpone presidential elections due on July 27.
"I believe that, on the whole, the authorities want to create incidents to prevent the presidential elections from taking place," he said.
Witnesses said at least six armoured cars had been deployed at about 4 a.m. in Brazzaville's northeastern Mpila district.
Tanks were on the streets in various parts of the capital later and soldiers wandered round firing in the air. The U.S. embassy advised its nationals to stay at home.

France has economic interests in the Central African nation and 350 troops there -- left overs from an operation to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa in the last days of the civil war in former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Brazzaville is just across the river from Kinshasa, capital of the former Zaire.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 following parliamentary elections in 1993.
Last Friday the government banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence.
Clashes between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango in their hometowns have killed 16 people in less than a month.

The government said it would pursue two senior members of Sassou Nguesso's guard it held responsible. A government statement on Wednesday night also threatened tough measures against anyone carrying an unauthorised weapon.
"Since five o'clock this morning there has been sustained shooting around my residence. There are about 10 armoured vehicles and infantry soldiers," Sassou Nguesso said.
"One of my security men has already received bullet wounds in the shoulder."
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. Frontrunners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and opposition leader Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.
Sassou Nguesso has not yet officially said he will run but he has campaigned widely since returning home in February.
Kolelas's supporters have made one southern, river-front area of the capital a no-go area for the army.

Lissouba defeated Kolelas in the second round of the 1992 election. Sassou Nguesso was eliminated in the first round with 16.87 percent, behind Lissouba with just under 36 percent and Kolelas with just under 23 percent.

Sassou Nguesso ran a notionally Marxist single-party administration until the advent of multi-party politics in the early 1990s. He then adopted an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and liberal economic policy.
